DEFINITION: Credit-claiming is a statement in which the senator asserts or implies personal (or shared) responsibility for a government action or outcome that benefits constituents—e.g., securing federal funds, delivering projects, passing legislation, getting an agency to act, or achieving a policy result.

CLARIFICATION: Include cases where the senator announces particularized benefits to their state/district (grants, funding, designations, disaster declarations, missions, facilities) since the announcement is a vehicle for claiming credit; where the senator claims to have authored, sponsored, offered, or secured provisions/amendments/legislation that were adopted or enacted; where the senator links their own actions (letters, requests, appeals, pressure, oversight) to a subsequent favorable government decision; where the senator claims their oversight/investigation produced results. The claim can be explicit ("I secured," "my amendment was included," "at my request") or implicit through juxtaposition (delegation requested X; agency then did X).

NEGATIVE CLARIFICATION: Exclude pure position-taking: statements of support/opposition on votes, policy debates, criticism of the administration/opponents, floor statements, op-eds. Exclude announcements of bill introductions/cosponsorship without enacted/adopted outcomes. Exclude advocacy/requests/letters where no favorable outcome has yet occurred and no past outcome is claimed. Exclude ceremonial items: condolences, commemorations, awards to others, event announcements, town meeting notices. Exclude welcoming/applauding others' actions without claiming a personal role (unless the release links the outcome to the senator's own efforts). Exclude attributing credit to others (e.g., crediting the President). Voting for a bill = position-taking, but claiming that one's own amendment/provision was included in passed legislation = credit-claiming.

DEFINITION: Credit-claiming is a statement in which the senator asserts or implies personal (or shared) responsibility for a government action or outcome that benefits constituents—e.g., securing federal funds, delivering projects, passing legislation, getting an agency to act, or achieving a policy result.

CLARIFICATION: Include cases where the senator announces particularized benefits to their state/district (grants, funding, designations, disaster declarations, missions, facilities) since the announcement is a vehicle for claiming credit; where the senator claims to have authored, sponsored, offered, or secured provisions/amendments/legislation that were adopted or enacted; where the senator links their own actions (letters, requests, appeals, pressure, oversight) to a subsequent favorable government decision; where the senator claims their oversight/investigation produced results. The claim can be explicit ("I secured," "my amendment was included," "at my request") or implicit through juxtaposition (delegation requested X; agency then did X).

NEGATIVE CLARIFICATION: Exclude pure position-taking: statements of support/opposition on votes, policy debates, criticism of the administration/opponents, floor statements, op-eds. Exclude announcements of bill introductions/cosponsorship without enacted/adopted outcomes. Exclude advocacy/requests/letters where no favorable outcome has yet occurred and no past outcome is claimed. Exclude ceremonial items: condolences, commemorations, awards to others, event announcements, town meeting notices. Exclude welcoming/applauding others' actions without claiming a personal role (unless the release links the outcome to the senator's own efforts). Exclude attributing credit to others (e.g., crediting the President). Voting for a bill = position-taking, but claiming that one's own amendment/provision was included in passed legislation = credit-claiming.
